candidates.title: Global Research Trends and Current Landscape of Allergen Immunotherapy for Allergic Rhinitis and Asthma: A Comprehensive Bibliometric Analysis
candidates.abstract: Abstract Background: Allergen Immunotherapy (AIT) is the only therapeutic approach that can alter the progression of immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated allergic disorders. It plays a crucial role in promoting immune tolerance and effectively managing allergic rhinitis (AR), asthma and venom hypersensitivity. Methods: This study conducted a systematic bibliometric analysis of global research in the field of AIT. A total of 1,718 relevant articles published from 2000 to 2025 were extracted from the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC; n = 1,718) and PubMed (n = 1,586), and in-depth analyses were performed using tools including CiteSpace, VOSviewer and Charticulator. Results: Annual publication volume has shown steady growth with significant acceleration since 2014. Additionally, the United States has dominated research output, European countries have formed a strong secondary cluster, and China has shown the fastest growth since 2017, while international collaborations formed a densely connected core with sparsely linked peripheral groups. Primary research focused on the management of AR and asthma, whereas studies of food allergy and atopic dermatitis contributed relatively little within an AR/asthma-anchored corpus. The comparative effectiveness of sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) and subcutaneous immunotherapy (SCIT) has emerged as a key focus in highly cited literature. The temporal evolution of keywords demonstrated a shift from traditional allergen extracts to molecularly characterized allergens, component-resolved diagnosis, and personalized immunotherapy approaches. Conclusion: This study comprehensively delineated the knowledge framework and translational challenges in global AIT research, specifically addressing issues in the translation of scientific achievements to clinical applications. Future research should focus on developing innovative delivery systems, optimizing treatment protocols, identifying predictive biomarkers, and conducting real-world evidence studies to effectively bridge the gap between scientific advancements and clinical implementation.

candidates.title: The Shifting Landscape of PRRSV-1 in China (2021–2025): Genetic Diversity and Emergence of Novel Subgroups
candidates.abstract: Background: The detection rate of European Porcine Reproductive and Respiratory Syndrome Virus (PRRSV-1) is increasing in China, and the epidemic and evolutionary situation are complex. Method: Extract 43 PRRSV-1 ORF5 sequences from 2021 to 2025, and conduct phylogenetic, recombination, and genetic distance analyses using LV and VR-2332 as outgroups. Result: BJEU06-1-like subgroup remained dominant (65.1%), while New subgroup 1 accounted for 2.3%; New subgroups 1 and 2 were discovered, and no recombination was detected within ORF5. The genetic distance between NMEU09-1 and the New subgroup 1 is the largest (nucleotide 0.231, amino acid 0.192). Conclusions: The epidemic pattern of PRRSV-1 is complex, and New subgroups have evolutionary potential. Monitoring, early warning, and comprehensive prevention and control should be strengthened.

candidates.title: Hashimoto’s thyroiditis through a tissue lens: cellular remodeling from follicular injury to inflammatory niche formation
candidates.abstract: Hashimoto’s thyroiditis (HT) is an organ-specific autoimmune disorder characterized by immune infiltration and progressive remodeling of thyroid follicular tissue. This review examines how inflammatory injury reshapes epithelial, stromal, vascular, and extracellular compartments and how these changes may influence persistence of thyroid damage. Evidence from human histology and ultrastructure, single-cell and spatial profiling, thyroid organoids, and experimental models is integrated to distinguish established tissue alterations from associative molecular signatures and experimentally supported mechanisms. At the epithelial level, HT is associated with heterogeneous thyrocyte injury, altered junctional organization, and changes in cell–matrix interactions. Stromal remodeling includes disease-associated fibroblast and myofibroblast states, collagen-rich extracellular matrix changes, and vascular alterations within inflammatory regions. Spatial studies further demonstrate that epithelial, immune, stromal, and endothelial populations are organized into distinct inflammatory neighborhoods. Mechanistic studies support cytokine-mediated disruption of epithelial barriers and adhesion-dependent survival signaling, together with context-dependent contributions from oxidative and autophagic stress, inflammasome-linked pyroptosis, immune-cell metabolic reprogramming, and regulatory non-coding RNAs. We propose an immune-primary structural-amplification hypothesis, to be tested rather than assumed: inflammation is the primary driver of thyroid injury, whereas subsequent remodeling of follicular architecture and the local microenvironment could modify epithelial vulnerability or inflammatory persistence. Whether remodeling independently worsens follicular injury remains unresolved. Important uncertainties concern temporal sequence, disease-stage heterogeneity, treatment status, and differences between circulating and intrathyroidal measurements. Longitudinal tissue studies, spatially resolved molecular profiling, perturbable thyroid organoids, and immune–stromal co-culture systems are needed to define which structural changes are causal modifiers, reversible consequences, or biomarkers of established disease. This tissue-centered perspective links cellular organization to disease progression within the limits of evidence.

candidates.title: Strain selection determines the morphology and silver loading of supernatant-mediated silver nanoparticles: evidence from bacteria isolated from an urban lake
candidates.abstract: Urban lakes in expanding Indian cities receive mixed domestic and agricultural inputs, and their culturable bacteria are of interest both as indicators of sanitary status and as a source of strains for applied biotechnology. A surface water sample from Doddagubbi Lake, Bengaluru, India, was examined by culture-dependent methods. The heterotrophic plate count on nutrient agar was 8.0 × 103 CFU mL-1. Presumptive coliforms were detected on eosin methylene blue agar, whereas Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Salmonella spp. and actinobacteria were not recovered. Three Gram-negative, motile, aerobic isolates (KJU0088, KJU0089 and KJU0090) were purified and characterised by colony morphology, staining, biochemical tests, UV–visible profiling of cell-free spent broth, antibiotic susceptibility and cross-streak assay. Two representative strains were identified by 16S rRNA gene sequencing as Citrobacter freundii KJU0088 (GenBank PZ682701) and Comamonas testosteroni KJU0089 (GenBank PZ682702). All three isolates were susceptible to ofloxacin, kanamycin and azithromycin and showed no mutual antagonism. Cell-free supernatants of all three isolates reduced 1 mM AgNO3 to a black colloid within 24 h. Field emission scanning electron microscopy with energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (FESEM–EDS) showed that, under an identical synthesis protocol, particle morphology and silver content differed between preparations: silver accounted for 40.1 ± 0.4, 23.1 ± 0.3 and 13.3 ± 0.3 wt% for KJU0088, KJU0089 and KJU0090, respectively, with the residual carbon and oxygen fraction rising as the silver fraction fell. The study provides baseline culturable-bacteria data for Doddagubbi Lake and shows that the morphology and silver loading of supernatant-mediated silver nanoparticles depend on the isolate used.

candidates.title: Multiscale temporality and immunometabolic reprogramming in gouty arthritis: a narrative review
candidates.abstract: Gout is a monosodium urate (MSU) crystal-associated autoinflammatory arthritis, yet the timing of its flares is not fully explained by crystal burden alone. Observational studies report an excess of attacks at night or in the early morning, whereas seasonal findings vary by geography, endpoint and treatment context. This narrative review integrates three temporal scales: within-day flare timing, within-year variation and longer-term heterogeneity in clinical presentations. It distinguishes clinical observations from mechanisms supported mainly by experimental or tissue-based studies, including urate handling, circadian regulation of inflammasome priming and activation, immune-cell metabolism and inflammatory resolution. We use phase, amplitude and baseline as descriptive, potentially measurable constructs rather than validated gout biomarkers or independent causal pathways. Sleep, medication timing, diet, hydration, physical activity, shift work and healthcare-seeking may confound observed temporal associations. Trained-immunity-like reprogramming remains a testable hypothesis, not an established cause of recurrent flares or tophus formation. The review distinguishes asymptomatic hyperuricaemia from established gout and separates guideline-supported care from investigational chronotherapy. The proposed framework generates testable research questions without assuming a universal disease sequence or a proven clock-time treatment effect.

candidates.title: Plant-Derived Compounds for Controlling Intestinal Carriage of Carbapenem-Resistant Enterobacterales: Evidence, Ecological Risks, and Translational Priorities
candidates.abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) colonize the intestinal tract, providing a reservoir for transmission and invasive infection. Plant-derived compounds are of interest, but their ability to control CRE while preserving protective microbiota remains uncertain. This narrative review examines antibacterial, antivirulence, antibiofilm, anti-conjugation and microbiota-related evidence relevant to intestinal CRE carriage. Evidence was critically assessed according to experimental model, chemical characterization, intestinal exposure, and microbial selectivity, with direct CRE findings distinguished from indirect evidence obtained in other organisms or disease models. Selected compounds and antibiotic combinations show activity against CRE in vitro; separate preclinical studies report effects on microbial metabolism and barrier function. No study identified in this review evaluated intestinal CRE carriage following treatment with a plant-derived intervention; therefore, its ability to achieve durable decolonization remains unestablished. Major gaps include achievable intestinal concentrations, effects on protective anaerobes, resistance-gene transfer and carriage after withdrawal. Reduced pathogen abundance and increased microbial diversity are each insufficient to demonstrate ecological protection. We propose a staged framework testing pathogen control, ecological preservation, resistance-related effects and safety as distinct outcomes, advancing candidates only when chemically reproducible preparations show activity in gut-community models and subsequent in vivo studies. Clinical value depends on direct evidence of durable carriage reduction alongside ecological and safety outcomes.

candidates.title: RNA deaminase modulates metabolic stress-induced longevity in Caenorhabditis elegans
candidates.abstract: Adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing expands transcriptomic diversity, yet its contribution to organismal aging remains unclear. Here, we show that ADAR enzyme ADR-2 is specifically required for lifespan extension under metabolic stress. Loss of adr-2 abolished the longevity of mitochondrial dysfunction (isp-1) and dietary restriction (eat-2) mutants, while leaving lifespan extension mediated by reduced insulin/IGF-1 (daf-2) or mTOR (rsks-1) signaling intact. RNA editome analysis revealed increased ADR-2-dependent editing of three paralogous transmembrane genes, trel-1, trel-2, and trel-3, in long-lived isp-1 and eat-2 animals. Deletion of these genes partially restored lifespan in adr-2-deficient mutants, establishing a genetic interaction between adr-2 and trel genes. TREL proteins localize to lysosome-related organelles, and loss of trel genes alters the intracellular distribution of a fluorescent heme analog. Consistent with this, the human TREL homolog MFSD7 (SLC49A3) displays similar lysosomal localization and influences heme analog compartmentalization. Together, these findings uncover a context-dependent role for ADR-2 in longevity and implicate TREL proteins as a regulatory node linking metabolic stress to intracellular heme homeostasis and lifespan regulation. Author summary: Aging is influenced by multiple genetic and environmental factors, yet the molecular mechanisms that connect metabolic stress to lifespan regulation remain incompletely understood. RNA editing is a post-transcriptional process that alters RNA sequences and can modify gene function without changing the underlying DNA. In this study, we investigated the role of A-to-I RNA editing in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans. We found that ADR-2 is specifically required for lifespan extension caused by mitochondrial dysfunction and dietary restriction, but not for longevity induced by reduced insulin or mTOR signaling. We identified three related genes, trel-1, trel-2, and trel-3, whose RNA editing was increased in the mitochondrial and dietary restriction models. Removing trel-1 and trel-2 together, or trel-3 alone, partially restored lifespan in these models when ADR-2 was absent. We further show that TREL proteins localize to lysosome-related organelles and influence the intracellular distribution of a fluorescent heme analog. A human homolog, SLC49A3, exhibits similar properties in cultured cells. Our findings reveal genetic interactions between adr-2 and trel genes in lifespan regulation and suggest a previously unrecognized connection between intracellular heme regulation and aging.

candidates.title: The Aspergillus fumigatus C2-domain protein SppA is required for septal integrity and alters susceptibility to echinocandins and neutrophil killing during infection
candidates.abstract: Aspergillus fumigatus is a major opportunistic fungal pathogen whose ability to maintain hyphal integrity and withstand host defenses is critical for virulence. Septal pores, which connect hyphal compartments, are dynamically regulated to preserve cellular integrity under stress, yet the molecular components governing this process remain incompletely defined. Here, we identify and characterize a septal pore-associated protein, SppA, and demonstrate its essential role in maintaining septal integrity in A. fumigatus. We show that expression of SppA is positively regulated by the transcription factor ZfpA and is induced in response to the cell wall-targeting antifungal caspofungin. Deletion of sppA resulted in defective septal organization and increased susceptibility to hyphal damage. The mutant exhibited heightened sensitivity to cell wall-targeting antifungal agents, indicating a role in cell wall stress tolerance. In a zebrafish model of invasive aspergillosis, loss of SppA significantly attenuated virulence which was abrogated in neutrophil-deficient zebrafish. Further, the mutant strain displayed increased susceptibility to killing by primary human neutrophils, suggesting that proper septal pore formation contributes to fungal survival during host immune attack. Together, our findings establish SppA as a critical determinant of septal integrity, antifungal tolerance, and pathogenicity in A. fumigatus, and position it as part of a ZfpA-regulated, caspofungin-responsive pathway that supports fungal survival during stress and infection. Author summary: Aspergillus fumigatus is a common environmental mold that can cause life-threatening infections in people with weakened immune systems. For successful invasion of host tissue, the fungus requires the ability to protection sections of its hyphae from cell wall targeting antifungals and host immune cell attack by closing septal (cross wall) pores distributed throughout hyphal strands. We have identified an A. fumigatus protein, SppA, required for proper septal pore closure. Loss of SppA reduces the ability of hyphae to withstand treatment with antifungals and the ability of A. fumigatus to cause disease in a zebrafish infection model. The SppA mutant was particularly susceptible to killing by neutrophils, key immune cells that help control fungal infections. Our findings reveal an important mechanism that helps A. fumigatus survive environmental and host-imposed stresses and highlight septal pore regulation as a potential target for future antifungal strategies.
