candidates.title: Species diversity increases information flow about predation in bird communities
candidates.abstract: by Agnishikhe Kumar, Jiahao Wu, Ping Ding, Jakob Bro-Jørgensen, Mylène Dutour, Ari E. Martínez, Xingfeng Si, Qiang Zhang, Eben Goodale The Biodiversity-Ecosystem Functioning (BEF) literature has shown species diversity to be essential for ecosystem functioning and services. Yet this concept has not been extended often to behavioral ecology, so that although it is understood that acquiring social information from heterospecific individuals is an important component of ecosystem functioning, it is unclear how animal signaling at the community level, and subsequent information flow, is related to increased species diversity. Eliciting vocal responses using predator models across 10 nature reserves on a latitudinal gradient, we first show that the species diversity of birds is correlated with signaling about predation, both in the low-risk system of mobbing and in the higher-risk system of alarm calls. After finding a similar result across a fragment area gradient in one reserve, we used this system to test how interspecific information flow is affected by species diversity. Potential mechanisms behind this effect include that species are complementary in the characteristics of their mobbing calls, so more species translates into more cumulative information, or there are higher signaling rates as more individuals are involved, or a specific keystone species is more likely to occur. This experiment varied the number of species producing mobbing calls (one, two, four, eight species), with two playback construction methods (standardizing call rate, as typical for BEF experiments, or letting it increase with species richness, as in natural assemblages). Heterospecific mobbing participation (number of vocal species, number of participating individuals), and responses (call rate, probability to call in the first minute and frequency range) increased with species richness. Construction method significantly interacted with species richness, as non-standardized exemplars showed accentuated response as species richness increased. These results match expectations that complementary differences among species in the acoustic characteristics of mobbing calls, and increased call rate, both contribute to the result. There was little evidence that the signals of one particular species changed the experimental result. The overall evidence thus supports the hypothesis that the species diversity of a community is a key component influencing the quantity and the characteristics of signaling and information flow inside it.

candidates.title: Characterization and heterologous expression of surface polysaccharides from pathogenic Enterococcus cecorum .
candidates.abstract: Pathogenic variants of the chicken gastrointestinal bacterium Enterococcus cecorum are of growing concern due to their ability to cause vertebral osteomyelitis, such as enterococcal spondylitis or "kinky back," when the bacteria infect the free thoracic vertebrae of broilers. Due to the elimination of prophylactic antibiotic feed treatment that was previously used to manage the disease, there is now a need to develop other strategies for preventing pathogenic E. cecorum infections. In this work, we describe the structural characterization of two antigenic targets, a capsular polysaccharide and a rhamnopolysaccharide. Highly conserved biosynthetic gene clusters encoding enzymes for both structures have previously been identified in pathogenic E. cecorum. We show that these polysaccharides, when present on the surface of either the native or a heterologous host, induce an immune response in broilers. Furthermore, antibodies present in those sera cross-react with different E. cecorum strains and can induce killing of the pathogen in opsonophagocytosis assays. The characterization and heterologous expression of highly immunodominant cell wall polysaccharides that are conserved across many pathogenic strains is an important step toward the development of a potential glycoconjugate vaccine against E. cecorum.IMPORTANCEEnterococcus cecorum is a bacterium normally found in the gut of healthy chickens. However, pathogenic varieties of E. cecorum expressing surface capsular polysaccharides can cause skeletal deformations in the bird if the infection becomes systemic. This leads to severe morbidity and mortality in chickens raised for meat production and to significant financial losses for poultry producers. These infections were once managed by the inclusion of antibiotics in chicken feed; but this practice has been discontinued due to concern over antibiotic resistance development. We have identified polysaccharides that are conserved on the surface of many pathogenic E. cecorum that induce protective cross-reactive immune responses in chickens when the polysaccharides are expressed on a benign bacterial carrier. As an alternative to antibiotics, this is an important first step toward the development of a vaccine that specifically targets many pathogenic E. cecorum isolates and may help to reduce financial losses while improving animal welfare.

candidates.title: KvrA promotes pulmonary persistence and systemic dissemination of hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae .
candidates.abstract: Hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae (hvKp) poses a severe threat to human health, with KvrA, a member of the SlyA family of MarR-type transcriptional regulators, previously shown to contribute to capsule production, hypermucoviscosity formation, and virulence in Klebsiella pneumoniae . However, whether KvrA coordinates additional surface-associated pathways during infection remains incompletely understood. This study systematically investigated the role of KvrA in the survival, dissemination, and colonization of hvKp through in vitro and in vivo experiments. We found that knocking out kvrA in K. pneumoniae KPPR1 resulted in a capsular-deficient phenotype in bacterial colonies. KvrA was confirmed to positively regulate the expression of capsular polysaccharide (CPS)-associated genes, thereby promoting the synthesis of CPS. The Δ kvrA mutant displayed reduced survival rate when exposed to human serum, and the amount of its biofilm formation also decreased. Furthermore, in vitro , macrophages significantly phagocytosed more Δ kvrA mutant than wild type, indicating that KvrA contributes to phagocytic resistance of hvKp. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed that KvrA regulates additional surface-associated pathways, including lipopolysaccharide (LPS) biosynthesis and type 3 fimbria-associated biofilm formation. A murine pneumonia infection model revealed that the Δ kvrA mutant exhibited higher bacterial clearance in the lung, liver, and spleen compared with the wild-type strain, indicating that KvrA contributes to in vivo survival, dissemination, and colonization of hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae (hvKp). Histopathological observations further corroborated the contribution of KvrA to hvKp pathogenicity in mice. Collectively, our findings extend previous studies by demonstrating that KvrA not only regulates capsule-associated virulence traits but also coordinates additional surface-associated pathways, including LPS biosynthesis and type 3 fimbria/biofilm-related processes, contributing to pulmonary persistence and systemic dissemination of hvKp.IMPORTANCE Klebsiella pneumoniae is an opportunistic pathogen that has emerged as a significant causative agent for both community-acquired and nosocomial infections. The emergence of highly virulent and multidrug-resistant strains of K. pneumoniae poses a substantial threat to public health. The gene kvrA plays a pivotal role in the colonization and pathogenicity of K. pneumoniae . Understanding the regulatory mechanisms of KvrA in K. pneumoniae provides a theoretical basis for identifying novel genetic targets to control K. pneumoniae infections, which may facilitate the development of therapeutic agents.

candidates.title: The mechanosensitive channel MscS links lipoteichoic acid synthesis alterations to beta-lactam sensitivity in Staphylococcus aureus .
candidates.abstract: Lipoteichoic acid (LTA) is an essential cell envelope polymer in Staphylococcus aureus and contributes to beta-lactam resistance in methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA). Mutations that alter LTA synthesis sensitize MRSA to beta-lactam antibiotics, but the mechanism connecting the envelope polymer defects to antibiotic susceptibility has remained unclear. Here, using suppressor mutants with a mutation in RNA polymerase subunits, we found that LTA synthesis defects increased expression of a ParB-like protein and the mechanosensitive channel MscS. This locus was repressed in RNA polymerase suppressor mutants, which restored beta-lactam resistance, whereas induced expression of both genes reduced resistance. Increased ParBL-MscS expression was associated with decreased intracellular potassium and reduced cyclic di-AMP (c-di-AMP), linking altered membrane-envelope physiology to second messenger signaling. LTA synthesis mutants also showed reduced production of penicillin-binding protein 4 (PBP4), an important determinant of beta-lactam resistance. Modest restoration of PBP4 improved resistance in the mutant with reduced LTA abundance, whereas the mutant producing elongated LTA showed a distinct response, indicating that different LTA defects impose different envelope stresses. Also, under reduced LTA conditions, increased c-di-AMP level alone was not sufficient to restore PBP4 expression and beta-lactam resistance. Together, these findings identify a potassium-dependent pathway connecting LTA synthesis, mechanosensitive channel activity, c-di-AMP signaling, PBP4 production, and beta-lactam resistance. This work reveals how cell envelope perturbations are converted into cytoplasmic regulatory responses that control antibiotic susceptibility and suggests that ion homeostasis and c-di-AMP signaling may be exploitable pathways for restoring beta-lactam efficacy against MRSA.IMPORTANCEAntibiotic-resistant Staphylococcus aureus , including methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA), is difficult to treat because it can withstand many beta-lactam antibiotics. Changes in lipoteichoic acid (LTA), a major cell-envelope polymer, increase beta-lactam sensitivity, but the underlying mechanism has been unclear. Here, we show that LTA synthesis defects activate a pathway involving the predicted membrane channel MscS. This pathway lowers intracellular potassium, reduces cyclic di-AMP signaling, and decreases production of PBP4, a cell-wall synthesis enzyme that contributes to beta-lactam resistance. These changes make MRSA more vulnerable to beta-lactam antibiotics. Our findings show that antibiotic resistance depends not only on drug targets but also on coordination between the cell envelope, ion homeostasis, and intracellular signaling. This connection identifies physiological pathways that may be exploited to restore beta-lactam efficacy against resistant S. aureus .

candidates.title: When should adaptation arise from a polygenic response versus few large-effect changes?
candidates.abstract: by William R. Milligan, Laura K. Hayward, Guy Sella When will adaptation involve a few genetic changes of large effect versus a polygenic response? There are compelling reasons to expect polygenic adaptation to be common, yet direct evidence is lacking. Conversely, there are hundreds of examples of large-effect adaptations across species, but it is unclear whether they occur frequently within any given species. These different lines of evidence are hard to synthesize, in part due to the lack of theory that relates them. To address this gap, we frame the question in terms of the properties of an adaptive trait. We ask how the genetic basis of adaptation depends on key aspects of genetic variation in the trait and on the degree to which its selection pressures have changed. To this end, we consider a quantitative trait subject to stabilizing selection and model its response when a population at mutation–selection–drift balance experiences a sudden shift in the trait optimum. Using this model, we delimit how the contributions of large-effect and polygenic changes to adaptation depend on the genetics and ecology of adaptive traits, as well as on other salient factors. Thus, we formulate testable predictions for when different modes of adaptation are expected.

candidates.title: Crop diversification promotes soil microbial carbon turnover.
candidates.abstract: Agricultural diversification alters plant residue chemistry and rhizodeposition, with legacy effects on soil organic matter (SOM) cycling. The priming effect (PE) and necromass formation are key processes of SOM dynamics, yet how diversification affects these processes, and SOM persistence remains poorly understood. Using 13C-labelled glucose in a 150-day incubation of soils (0-15 cm) from two contrasting diversification trials (43 and 8 years), we found that diversification increased SOM priming by 153-174% and retention of glucose-derived 13C in microbial necromass by 227-289%. Diversified soils also had more bioavailable C, dissolved organic C, and neutral sugars, stronger stoichiometric nutrient limitation (103% higher C:P imbalance and 15% lower vector angle), and higher microbial activity and N- and P-acquiring enzyme activities. Microbial C use efficiency increased by 65%, while replacing the native microbial community of diversified soils with that of conventional soils reduced CUE by 9% and 45% at the 43- and 8-year sites, respectively. Community-level analyses further linked greater retention of glucose-derived 13C in microbial necromass to putative Discosea and Bacillota co-occurrence patterns. Metagenomic profiling revealed 18-125% higher relative abundances of CAZyme genes involved in degrading plant- and microbial-derived compounds, alongside a modest (~4%) increase in Y-associated functional potential at both sites. Although priming-induced native-C losses exceeded the amount of glucose-derived 13C retained in microbial necromass, the ratio of necromass C retention to priming-induced C loss was 28% higher under diversification than under conventional cropping over the 150-day incubation. Crop diversification thus reshapes microbial C cycling, coupling enhanced native SOM mineralization with greater retention of added C in microbial necromass, making the net effect on SOC dependent on sustained C inputs.

candidates.title: Non-enzymatic assimilation of organosulfur compounds at the interface of geochemistry and biochemistry.
candidates.abstract: Dimethyl sulfide (DMS) and dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) have important microbial-driven roles in global nutrient cycling, chemotaxis and/or climate regulation. Microbial DMSO and DMS assimilation were thought to require their enzymatic reduction to methanethiol. However, reactive oxygen species were recently shown to mediate methane production from DMS and DMSO. Here, we show that this oxidative mechanism can sustain microbial growth without the need for enzymes to directly reduce DMS or oxidize DMSO. In an interplay with iron, both light and heat were effective geochemical drivers of this mechanism that yielded methanesulfonic acid and sulfite, and which mimicked the stepwise oxidation of DMSO by monooxygenases that only enzymatically enhance this oxidation reaction. Furthermore, we demonstrated intracellular DMSO degradation, in which sulfur and the simultaneously released carbon were both utilized by microbes. This study emphasizes that metabolic pathways are not necessarily enzyme-driven, with putatively ancient, non-enzymatic reaction networks taking place at a transition between geochemistry and biochemistry.

candidates.title: Environmental microbial exposure as an under-measured exposome domain: Links to host microbiomes, immune regulation, and disease epidemiology.
candidates.abstract: Environmental microbial exposure is an under-measured biological component of the exposome and a plausible determinant of immune-mediated disease patterns. Humans encounter microbial communities and products from soil, air, water, vegetation, animals, food systems, farms, indoor dust, healthcare settings, schools, and urban built environments. These exposures may influence gut, skin, airway, oral, and mucosal microbiomes and thereby alter epithelial barrier function, immune tolerance, inflammatory thresholds, and microbial metabolite production. This structured mechanistic narrative review integrates direct environmental-exposure studies, environment-to-host microbiome studies, host-microbiome mechanistic evidence, and translational frameworks. The clearest convergence occurs in asthma and allergic disease, where early-life farm exposure, endotoxin-rich dust, environmental microbial diversity, innate immune modulation, and epithelial A20 regulation support a coherent exposure-response model. Evidence for inflammatory bowel disease and broader respiratory outcomes is biologically credible but less direct, whereas metabolic and systemic inflammatory outcomes remain largely supported by host-microbiome and metabolite mechanisms rather than direct environmental exposure studies. The review therefore distinguishes evidence maturity and mechanistic proximity rather than treating all disease categories equally. It further positions pollution, urbanization, building design, biodiversity loss, diet, antibiotics, and socioeconomic conditions as active modifiers of microbial exposure and host response. Future studies should integrate direct environmental sampling with body-site microbiome profiling, functional multi-omics, immune and barrier biomarkers, geospatial exposure assessment, source tracking, repeated measures, and explicit causal-inference designs. Environmental microbial exposure should be treated neither as uniformly beneficial nor harmful, but as a measurable, context-dependent exposome domain whose health effects depend on composition, dose, timing, route, co-exposures, and host susceptibility.
candidates.journal: Journal of environmental health science & engineering

candidates.title: Single-molecule whole-genome sequencing reveals genomic and epigenomic concordance between ultrasonic aspiration and surgical resection in meningioma: prospective feasibility series.
candidates.abstract: Background Ultrasonic surgical aspirators, including Sonopet ® , are widely used during skull base meningioma resection to enable safe tumor debulking in constrained corridors, but aspirated tumor fragments are often discarded. Whether this tissue supports genomic and epigenomic profiling comparable to standard resection tissue is unknown. The aim of this study was to determine whether Sonopet ® aspirate is a viable substrate for long-read genomic and epigenomic profiling in skull base meningioma. Methods We prospectively collected paired standard resection (R) and Sonopet ® aspirate (S) specimens from seven patients with skull base meningioma and performed Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) long-read whole-genome sequencing using PromethION R10 flow cells. We compared sequencing yield, read quality, tumor purity, copy-number profiles, somatic single-nucleotide variant (SNV) burden, variant allele frequency, and CpG methylation between matched samples, then projected methylation profiles onto a reference framework of 121 EPIC array-profiled samples for molecular group classification. Results Aspirates generated sequencing yields, read lengths, and tumor purity comparable to matched specimens. Copy-number profiles were largely concordant and recovered canonical meningioma alterations, with close agreement in total and loss burden (Lin's CCC = 0.99, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.00). SNV burden showed moderate agreement (CCC = 0.53, 95% CI - 0.28 to 0.99), with two discordant patients possibly reflecting intratumoral heterogeneity. Promoter methylation was closely correlated between pairs (Pearson r > 0.99 across ~ 177,000 promoters), and molecular group classification was concordant in all pairs except P1, where tumor purity was uncertain. Conclusions Sonopet ® aspirate provides tissue comparable to standard resection specimens for long-read genomic and epigenomic profiling, supporting its use as a substrate for molecular diagnosis and translational research, particularly for subtotally resected tumors with limited tissue.

candidates.title: Mitochondrial Phylogeny Reveals Deep Intraspecific Divergence and Fine-Scale Regional Structure in Orangutans.
candidates.abstract: Orangutans ( Pongo spp.) are a valuable model for investigating how past climatic and geological events have shaped population structure and species diversification. We reconstructed 237 complete mitochondrial genomes from whole-genome sequencing data and combined them with 50 available mitochondrial sequences, resulting in a dataset of 287 orangutans spanning the current range of Sumatran and Bornean orangutans. Among Sumatran orangutans ( P. abelii ), we identified five geographically distinct mitochondrial clades corresponding to Langkat, North Aceh, Tripa, West Leuser and Batu Ardan. These clades showed strong differentiation, indicating long-term persistence of distinct maternal lineages across the Leuser landscape. For the recently described species, P. tapanuliensis , we added 10 newly reconstructed mitogenomes, increasing representation from 3 to 13 individuals. P. tapanuliensis formed a monophyletic, deeply divergent clade, confirming strong mitochondrial differentiation and long-term isolation. In Bornean orangutans ( P. pygmaeus ), we identified seven major regional mitochondrial clades corresponding to Sarawak, Central Kalimantan, South Kalimantan, Southeast Kalimantan, East Kalimantan and the North and South Kinabatangan populations in Sabah. Within the subspecies P. p. morio , the North and South Kinabatangan, East Kalimantan and Southeast Kalimantan clades formed distinct maternal lineages, revealing substantial mitochondrial structure within the currently recognised subspecies. Our findings suggest that current geographic and taxonomic divisions may under-represent the extent of regional maternal diversity across orangutans. Female philopatry has preserved ancient mitochondrial structure across Sundaland, with its geographic distribution shaped by refugial persistence, major riverine barriers and long-term population fragmentation.

candidates.title: Inbreeding in the genomics era: comparing IBD, drift, and homozygosity-based methods in a pig breeding population.
candidates.abstract: Background The inbreeding and kinship methods can be classified into three approaches: (1) Identity-by-Descent (IBD) estimates the probability that alleles are identical by shared ancestry; (2) Drift-based methods measure deviations in allele frequencies from a base due to genetic drift; and (3) Homozygosity-based (HOM) methods estimate genome-wide homozygosity. The objective of this study was to compare the estimated inbreeding and kinship rates using those three approaches. Within each approach, different methods were investigated. The dataset consisted of purebred sires from artificial insemination centers born between 2014 and 2024, along with their relatives with genotype data, totaling 152,883 pigs. Animals were genotyped with various SNP panels and imputed to medium- and high-density panels (50 K and 660 K). Results For inbreeding estimates, correlations among IBD-based methods were high (0.88), while correlations among drift-based methods ranged from 0.74 to 0.91. Homozygosity-based estimates showed a wide range of correlations (- 0.03 to 1.00). This variability was mainly driven by low or negative correlations involving short runs of homozygosity (ROH) classes (2-4 Mb and 4-8 Mb), which showed poor agreement with longer ROH categories. Correlations between methods from different approaches were generally weak to high (- 0.09 to 0.81). Kinship estimates showed higher correlations than inbreeding estimates. Nevertheless, the same pattern was observed: correlations were consistently higher within the same approach (above 0.96) than across different approaches (above 0.70). Rates of inbreeding and kinship per generation, estimated as regression slopes across birth years and converted to a per-generation scale, were consistently higher for drift-based measures than for the other approaches. This indicates that drift-based and homozygosity-based measures are not equivalent under genomic selection. Their differences are proportional to the covariance between changes in allele frequency and initial allele frequencies. Consequently, minor alleles tend to increase in frequency more often than expected under neutrality in this pig breeding line. Conclusions Overall, the results show that different approaches to estimating inbreeding and kinship convey distinct biological information. Homozygosity-based measures yielded lower estimates than drift-based metrics, suggesting non-neutral dynamics of allele frequencies. These findings indicate that constraining inbreeding using a drift-based genomic relationship matrix within an optimum contribution selection scheme may improve the management of genetic diversity.

candidates.title: Gray bats heighten their response to social cues when navigating group flight in environments with obstacles.
candidates.abstract: Bats are fast fliers with great maneuverability. Many species sense and communicate through echolocation, relying on acoustic signals in the environment. Bats also form large colonies, which necessitates that they fly in groups. When group size increases or obstacles are in their flight paths, the acoustic space can become cluttered, posing a non-trivial challenge for navigation. How do they interact with their environment and conspecifics, and how do they balance social and environmental cues? Recent research has uncovered individual adaptations to calling and flight patterns when flying in the groups or avoiding obstacles. Studies also suggest coordination when foraging, as well as strategies used by the group to mitigate acoustic clutter. However, there has yet to be a study on how bats weigh different navigational tasks when flying in spatially complex environments. Here, we collected stereoscopic video data from a wild colony of gray bats, Myotis grisescens, navigating their usual foraging flight paths in the presence of novel obstacles. We find that bats tend to stay close to a wall, but space out when flying in groups. We develop a data-informed agent-based model which reveals that their social repulsive behavior is strengthened when challenged to navigate novel obstacles.

candidates.title: Explainable machine learning-assisted exploration of chromatin dynamics reveals chromosome-specific response to serum starvation.
candidates.abstract: Chromatin is dynamic at all length scales, influencing chromatin-based processes, such as gene expression. Even large-scale reorganization of whole chromosome territories has been reported upon specific signals, but the lack of suitable methods has prevented analysis of the underlying dynamic processes. Here, we have used CRISPR-Sirius for time-lapse imaging of chromatin loci dynamics during serum starvation. We show that chromosome 1 loci move toward the nuclear envelope during the first hour of serum starvation in a chromosome-specific manner. Machine learning-assisted exploration of acquired multiparametric data combined with the Shapley values-based explanation approach allowed us to uncover the critical features that characterize chromatin dynamics during serum starvation. This analysis reveals that although serum starvation affects overall nuclear morphology and chromatin dynamics, chromosome 1 loci display a specific response that is characterized by maintenance of dynamics in a constrained environment, and long 'jumps' at the nuclear periphery. Interestingly, the two homologous chromosomes display differential behaviors, with the more peripheral homolog being more responsive to the signal than the internal one. Overall, the presented machine learning-assisted dataset exploration helps us navigate the multidimensional data to understand the underlying dynamic processes and can be applied to a wide variety of research questions in imaging and cell biology in general.

candidates.title: Rethinking laboratory sustainability.
candidates.abstract: Green lab initiatives like My Green Lab and LEAF (Laboratory Efficiency Assessment Framework), are paving the way towards sustainable research by promoting resource efficiency, energy conservation, and waste reduction through behavioral changes. However, these initiatives focus almost exclusively on material consumption, overlooking deeper facets of scientific waste that stem from questionable research practices: the environmental cost of unnecessary or poorly designed experiments, discarded null results, unreproducible research, and distorted reporting. I argue that a more meaningful discussion of scientific sustainability must look beyond physical resource management to examine the scientific process itself; to rethink the questions we ask, the experiments we do, and how we communicate our findings. To build a truly sustainable scientific ecosystem, Green Lab initiatives must join forces with Open Science and research integrity movements to update not only the hardware, but also the software of science.

candidates.title: Junctional and actomyosin dynamics drive endothelial cell rearrangements during vascular tube formation.
candidates.abstract: Lumen formation is a key process during the morphogenesis of tubular organs, such as the vertebrate vascular network. At the cellular level, lumen formation can be achieved by cell shape changes or cell rearrangements. We have previously shown that such cell rearrangements are driven by oscillating membrane protrusions, called junction-based lamellipodia (JBL), which provide a ratchet mechanism driving convergent cell movements to connect local lumens, and generate vascular patency. By performing in vivo time-lapse imaging at high spatiotemporal resolution in zebrafish embryos, we have analyzed the cytoskeletal and junctional dynamics, which underlie JBL formation and function. We show that JBL formation requires the activity of the F-actin nucleation complex Arp2/3. We further show that a novel junction is formed at the distal end of the JBL from a pool of VE-cadherin originating from outside the initial JBL area. Subsequently, proximal and distal junctions merge and fuse, a process driven by actomyosin contractility. Prior to this fusion, we observe a specific recruitment of Myl9 within the interjunctional space. Furthermore, inhibition of actomyosin contractility abrogates junctional merging. Taken together, our analyses demonstrate that JBL constitute a module, which, by alternate generation of pushing forces (JBL formation) and pulling forces (junctional merging), provide the physical means for endothelial cells to elongate and to rearrange and thereby generate a continuous vascular lumen.

candidates.title: Diurnal rhythmicity in metabolism and salivary effector expression shapes aphid performance on host plants.
candidates.abstract: Diurnal rhythms influence insect behavior, physiology, and metabolism, optimizing their performance by adapting to daily changes in the environment. While their impact on agricultural pests has been briefly explored, our understanding of how these rhythms drive adaptive responses in pest biology and influence host colonization remains elusive. Here, we show that a notorious global aphid pest, Rhopalosiphum padi , exhibits distinct diurnal patterns in feeding behavior, with elevated honeydew excretion at night and extended phloem salivation during early nighttime. Temporal aphid transcriptome profiling reveals four diurnally rhythmic clusters, two of which peak at night, exhibiting enrichment in carbohydrate and amino acid metabolism. Beyond the established role in manipulating host responses and allowing sustained feeding, our study reveals novel evidence of cyclical fluctuations in salivary effector expression in an insect species. Silencing key effector genes, peaking in expression during the increased nighttime salivation, results in a more pronounced reduction in aphid excretion activity on host plants during the night compared to the day, a phenomenon not observed on artificial diets. A better understanding of aphid diurnal rhythms and their roles in shaping aphid performance provides a promising avenue to refine and optimize pest management, granting a strategic advantage for minimizing crop damage.

candidates.title: Adaptive sampling: information-guided selection for targeted long-read sequencing and epigenetic studies.
candidates.abstract: Adaptive sampling (AS) is a unique feature of nanopore sequencing that enables real-time enrichment or depletion of target molecules during the sequencing run based on their initial sequence information. AS provides a flexible and scalable alternative to conventional capture- and amplification-based approaches, while preserving long reads and the ability to detect epigenetic modifications of native DNA/RNA molecules. In this review, we summarize the principles of AS-based sequencing, explain the enrichment- and depletion-mode strategies and discuss factors affecting its performance. We further highlight the growing body of studies demonstrating the utility of AS across a diverse range of applications, such as metagenomic and microbiome research, structural variant characterization and discovery, studying repeat expansion disorders, integrated genetic and epigenetic profiling or transcriptome analysis. In these and other contexts, AS enables efficient allocation of sequencing capacity toward biologically relevant molecules, while accelerating data generation, which also makes it applicable to rapid molecular diagnostics and real-time genomic analyses in clinical practice. As nanopore sequencing continues to mature and become a standard analysis approach in many laboratories, AS is likely to evolve from a specialized enrichment strategy into a routine component of genomic, epigenomic, and transcriptomic workflows.

candidates.title: GEI-17-mediated SUMOylation of GDP dissociation inhibitor GDI-1 regulates apoptotic cell clearance
candidates.abstract: by Lei Yuan, Peiyao Li, Aiying Ma, Chao Li, Fuqiao Liu, Yunmin Xie, Qian Zheng, Hui Wang, Hui Xiao Apoptotic cell clearance represents the final stage of apoptosis and involves phagosome formation, maturation, and digestion. Here, we found that SUMO modifications participate in apoptotic cell clearance by influencing phagosomal degradation activity in C. elegans . The SUMO E3 ligase, GEI-17, SUMOylates GDP dissociation inhibitor (GDI-1) at K270 to trigger phagosomal degradation. Upon SUMOylation, GDI-1 facilitates release of GDP-bound RAB-1, which is subsequently converted to the GTP-bound form in a manner dependent on GDI displacement factor, PRAF-3. RAB-1 conversion enables binding and translocation of RAB-7 from the endoplasmic reticulum to Golgi to promote phagosome maturation and degradation activity. In the absence of GDI-1 SUMOylation, GDI-1 binds to GDP-RAB-1, sequestering it in the cytoplasm, resulting in impaired phagosomal degradation. Furthermore, we found SUMOylation of GDI1 at a conserved site plays a crucial role in efferocytosis regulation in mammals. This study defines a previously unrecognized mechanism by which SUMOylation drives apoptotic cell clearance.

candidates.title: Local feedback governs cell fate transition to drive self-organized phenotypic equilibrium in hierarchical tumors
candidates.abstract: by Emma Legait, Charlotte Rulquin, Lauranne Bouteille, Raphaël Clément, Cédric Maurange How cell-state transitions are regulated along a tumor lineage to determine its overall cellular composition remains unclear. Using a simple hierarchical tumor model in Drosophila , we show that differentiation of cancer stem cells (CSCs) into transit amplifying progenitors (TAPs) depends on the fraction of TAPs among their immediate neighbors. This relationship is captured by a local feedback transition rule that quantitatively predicts CSC transition probability. Implementing this rule in 3D growth simulations spontaneously recapitulates CSC clustering and the emergence of a stable CSC fraction within tumors. Mechanistically, the local feedback is mediated by EGFR signaling from newly produced TAPs, propagating differentiation across CSC clusters. Consistently, we show that clustering protects the CSC pool from depletion driven by surrounding TAPs, indicating that spatial architecture and lineage dynamics are tightly coupled. Together, these findings show that a local feedback governing fate transitions drives emergent spatial organization that stabilizes the stem cell fraction in hierarchical tumors.

candidates.title: Migration as a key influence on ungulate eco-evolutionary history
candidates.abstract: by Gustavo Burin Species can overcome resource limitations by migrating to more favourable areas. A new study in PLOS Biology shows that migration has an important effect on the diversification dynamics of ungulates, that likely led to changes in ecosystem functioning. Species can overcome environmental limitations by migrating to more favorable areas. This Primer explores a new study in PLOS Biology showing that this behavior has an important effect on the diversification dynamics of ungulates, which in turn likely led to changes in ecosystem properties and functioning.

candidates.title: An indirect wing steering muscle stabilizes flight by regulating wing pitch angle in Drosophila
candidates.abstract: by Han Kheng Teoh, Debojyoti Biswas, Haoru Li, Abby Leung, B. Kemper Ludlow, Samuel C. Whitehead, Erica Ehrhardt, Michael Dickinson, Tsevi Beatus, Noah J. Cowan, Itai Cohen Flapping flight is inherently unstable, requiring Drosophila to fine-tune their wing motions on a milliseconds timescale. Pioneering studies have shown that the direct steering muscles, which attach to the wing hinge, are important for generating these rapid flight reflexes. Recent connectome data, however, reveal that indirect steering muscles or tension muscles, which alter the mechanics of the thorax, receive some of the same synaptic inputs from the sensory apparatus as the direct steering muscles. This discovery suggests that the indirect steering muscles may also be important for flight control. Here, we show that the indirect tergopleural muscles indeed contribute substantially to stabilization, particularly for large pitch perturbations. We find that for small perturbations (less than 1,000 °/s), flies modulate their wing stroke amplitude to generate lift-based corrective torques, a strategy that has been previously documented. For larger perturbations, however, we observe that Drosophila engage an additional wing degree of freedom—the wing pitch angle—to leverage additional lift and drag forces during the corrective maneuver. Quasi-steady aerodynamic simulations reveal that this strategy minimizes power consumption, anaolgous to how some mammals (including humans) adjust their steady-state gaits in a near energy-optimal manner. Using optogenetics and a control theory framework, we demonstrate that the tergopleural muscle is activated by a proportional gain component of a nonlinear proportional-integral controller responsible for determining the wing pitch angle during large perturbations. A simplified torsional spring model for the wing hinge captures the changes in the wing pitch dynamics observed during correction maneuvers by using the tergopleural muscle to adjust the rest angle of the wing. These findings provide a striking example of reflex strategy selection in time-critical behaviors and underscore the vital role of indirect steering muscles in flight stabilization.

candidates.title: Plasma biomarkers of Alzheimer's disease reveal conserved features of age-related neurodegeneration in chimpanzees and humans
candidates.abstract: Aging is a major risk factor for Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (AD/ADRD). Yet, the physiological relationships linking age-related changes in peripheral biomarkers and measures of brain structure have only recently begun to be explored. Nonhuman primates, whose brains naturally express some of the pathologic hallmarks of AD/ADRD, including amyloid-beta (A{beta}) plaques, vascular amyloid, and neurofibrillary tangles, represent a critical translational bridge between rodent models and humans. Here, we utilized ultrasensitive multiplex assays and structural MRI to examine the relationship of plasma AD/ADRD biomarkers with age, sex, and whole brain cortical thickness (CT) and gray matter volume (GMV) in a cohort of chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes), humans' closest extant living relatives. Plasma levels (pg/ml) of total tau, phosphorylated tau 217 (pTau217), A{beta}40, A{beta}42, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), and neurofilament light chain (NfL) were measured in a cross-sectional sample of 154 chimpanzees ranging from 12-57 years of age. As in humans, aging was associated with increased plasma total tau, pTau217, A{beta}40, A{beta}42, GFAP, and NfL levels, as well as reduced whole brain CT and GMV in chimpanzees. The ratio of plasma A{beta}42/A{beta}40 increased with age in male chimpanzees, whereas aging was not significantly associated with the ratio of pTau217/A{beta}42. Mediation analyses revealed that age-related increases in plasma A{beta}42 mediated whole brain GMV atrophy in chimpanzees. Together, these findings demonstrate that plasma AD/ADRD biomarkers and measures of brain structure undergo age-related changes in chimpanzees, which is highly relevant to the study of human aging and AD/ADRD.

candidates.title: Nuclear phylogenomics illuminates deep lineage divergence and complex evolutionary histories in Dipsacales
candidates.abstract: Relationships among the five subfamilies of Linnina within Dipsacales remain contentious. Extensive nuclear gene-tree discordance and cytonuclear discordance involving Linnaeoideae complicate reconstruction of their early evolutionary history. We analyzed whole-genome resequencing data from 88 Dipsacales species representing all nine subfamilies and eight outgroups. Using Dipsacales-specific nuclear reference locus sets, we recovered 3,023 orthologous nuclear loci. Nuclear analyses consistently placed (Morinoideae + Zabelioideae) sister to (Linnaeoideae + (Valerianoideae + Dipsacoideae)) across inference methods and character-coding schemes. Despite strong backbone support, extensive gene-tree discordance persisted at deep nodes. Node-level analyses suggested that incomplete lineage sorting (ILS) was a major source of discordance, while evidence for ancient gene flow varied among nodes. At the Linnaeoideae + (Valerianoideae + Dipsacoideae) node, topology frequencies approached ILS-only expectations, whereas internal branch lengths supported a model incorporating gene flow. At the Morinoideae + Zabelioideae node, multiple analyses provided more consistent evidence of ancient gene flow. ILS-only simulations recovered the observed plastid placement of Linnaeoideae in 8.63% of replicates, indicating that ILS could generate this topology; ancient gene flow, potentially involving plastid capture, remains a possible explanation for the cytonuclear discordance. Divergence-time estimates placed four major Linnina backbone divergences between 56.87 and 48.77 Ma. These findings suggest that early Linnina diversification involved successive lineage divergences and extensive ancestral polymorphism sorting, potentially accompanied by ancient gene exchange among some ancestral lineages.

candidates.title: Revisiting homoploid hybrid speciation in Australian cotton (Gossypium) species
candidates.abstract: One of the earliest described cases of putative homoploid hybrid speciation was 35 years ago for the Australian cotton species, Gossypium bickii. This inference was based on discordance between chloroplast- and nuclear-based phylogenetic reconstructions, a type of incongruence that has become a relatively common observation in plants. Here we reevaluate evidence bearing on the evolutionary history of G. bickii in the context of an expanded sampling of all but one of the 17 described Australian cotton species, using whole-genome resequencing data based on 18,784 single-copy nuclear genes and entire plastome sequences. Genome-wide phylogenomic analyses resolved three well-defined sections (Sturtia, Hibiscoidea and Grandicalyx) and recapitulate the previously reported discordance between nuclear and plastid phylogenies. Although plastome inferences mirror phylogenetic discordance inferred earlier for G. bickii and G. cunninghamii, genome-wide nuclear data did not reveal compelling signals of interspecific introgression, perhaps because of population genetic nuclear swamping by a quantitatively larger paternal population and by subsequent genomic divergence. All analyses, including genome-wide phylogenetics and dating estimation, support a narrative in which there was early and rapid diversification of the three Australian sections, accompanied by early intersectional reticulation of plastomes without residual evidence in the nuclear genome.

candidates.title: RAMA: a global genome size database of invasive tetrapod species
candidates.abstract: Motivation: Rising numbers of biological invasions have triggered widespread erosion of environmental and socio-economic stability worldwide. To predict and understand the impacts of current and future invasive non-native species (INNS), invasion science has increased collective efforts to elucidate the role of functional traits as drivers of INNS establishments and impacts. Tetrapod vertebrates (reptiles, amphibians, mammals and birds) represent exceptionally well-studied animal lineages with broad data availability, while serving as regular model systems on the predictors of invasion success and impacts. However, while efforts exist to compile data on phenotypic traits, the availability of databases linking phenotypes and genomes remains neglected among animals. Here, we introduce the Reptilia, Amphibia, Mammalia and Aves (RAMA) database, an open-access, global-scale resource compiling genome size records for 3,539 non-native species together with invasion success and impact data. RAMA reveals relatively low coverage of tetrapod genome sizes (9.51%), as well as highlighting an imbalance in genomic and invasion data availability among taxa. Genome data is more commonly available for mammals (18.56%) and birds (16.42%) than for amphibians (5.1%) and reptiles (2.42%). RAMA, the first database to assemble animal genome size and invasion data together, encourages further investigations and incorporations of a genomic perspective within invasion science to develop predictive research and inform proactive management strategies. Main types of variables contained: species-level genome and invasion records. location and grain: Global, tetrapod-wide. Time period and grain: Extant (1883 to 2024). Major taxa and level of measurement: 3,539 tetrapod species. Software format: .csv

candidates.title: Genotype and environment shape gene regulatory variation in switchgrass
candidates.abstract: Local adaptation is contingent on genotype-by-environment interactions, which are often mediated by variation in gene expression. The causes and consequences of variation in gene expression are complex, and they are rarely evaluated under the multi-dimensional environmental regimes that occur in the field. Here, we investigate switchgrass gene expression variation in contrasting sites in Michigan and Texas. We examined differentially expressed genes between upland and lowland switchgrass genotypes and found that genes with genotype x environment (GxE) interactions were enriched for GO terms related to phosphorus metabolism. After mapping expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) in a switchgrass diversity panel in both sites, we compared distinct categories of eQTL to investigate their effects on gene expression in contrasting environments and their evolutionary history. Cis regulatory variants are more likely to have consistent effects across sites, while trans regulatory variants were more likely to have site-specific effects, and are more likely to underlie changes in gene expression between sites. Lower minor allele frequency in trans regulatory variants is consistent with stronger purifying selection. Furthermore, site-specific regulatory variants exhibited intermediate minor allele frequencies, consistent with balancing selection or soft sweeps. Finally, motivated by enrichment for phosphorus-related genes exhibiting differential expression between sites, we conducted a GWAS for leaf phosphorus concentration in the diversity panel. By overlaying the GWAS results with the eQTL map, we characterized cis and trans regulation of candidate genes for leaf P concentration in Michigan and Texas. Together, this work provides novel insights on the molecular basis and evolutionary history of GxE interactions in switchgrass.

candidates.title: A field-potential signature of pre-burst dynamics in human higher-order thalamic neurons
candidates.abstract: The aperiodic (1/f) component of the local field potential (LFP), long dismissed as noise, is increasingly being recognized as physiologically meaningful. Its exponent has been proposed to index excitation:inhibition (E:I) balance, with higher exponents (steeper spectra) corresponding to greater inhibition. Yet this hypothesis remains debated and has seldom been tested against single-neuron activity. Here, we used rare concurrent single-neuron and LFP recordings from the human pulvinar during goal-directed behavior and quiet wakefulness. Pulvinar recordings in both states revealed signatures of low-threshold calcium spikes (LTS) bursting. Prior work with intracellular recordings have established that LTS bursts require a sustained, spike-free period of hyperpolarization followed by a triggering depolarization, offering a physiologically-grounded test of the E:I hypothesis. We found that the exponent was higher during pre-burst silence relative to duration-matched silent windows preceding tonic spikes. The exponent also reflected the graded nature of burst-priming hyperpolarization: bursts with more constituent spikes followed longer silences and higher exponent peaks. Whereas these relationships held in both behavioral states, co-bursting across neurons exceeded chance only during goal-directed behavior. Co-bursts occurred on a slow (~100 ms) timescale, consistent with a shared cortical input mechanism, and were preceded by a larger rise in the exponent. Together, by linking a field potential measure to a known cellular mechanism, our findings show that the aperiodic exponent tracks the graded priming of thalamic bursts, providing human single-neuron support for the E:I hypothesis.

candidates.title: Spatial Transcriptomics Reveals Age-Specific Cancer Hallmark Architecture in Pediatric and Adult Brain Tumors
candidates.abstract: Pediatric cancers are fundamentally different from their adult counterparts. Specifically, pediatric cancers carry fewer mutations, interact with developing immune systems, and have active developmental microenvironments. The tumor microenvironment (TME), which includes the surrounding stromal cells, immune cells, blood vessels, and extracellular matrix, plays a crucial role in cancer progression, metastasis, behavior, and treatment response. To better understand the effects of the pediatric tumor microenvironment on tumor gene expression, we acquired spatial transcriptomic data from 17 pediatric brain tumor samples and analyzed it through a Cancer Hallmarks framework. Cancer Hallmarks, as outlined by Hanahan and Weinberg, provide a comprehensive set of 14 biological capabilities that cancers acquire to enable tumor growth and metastasis. We compared the spatial gene expression patterns of the Cancer Hallmarks gene sets between the TME and neoplastic compartments in pediatric brain tumors. Compared with a similar study of adult brain tumors, in which Cancer Hallmark expression patterns clearly separated the TME and neoplastic compartments, we identified three hallmarks ("Deregulating Cellular Energetics," "Senescent Cells," and "Evading Growth Suppressors") whose predominant cellular compartments differed between pediatric and adult tumors. In pediatric samples, these hallmarks were associated primarily with the TME rather than the neoplastic compartment. This shift implicates an age-specific rewiring of the tumor ecosystem. We also provide clear evidence of strong transcriptomic regulation in genes shared by pediatric and adult neoplastic compartments. Finally, we show how measures of spatial autocorrelation may be used to distinguish tumor grade.

candidates.title: Bidirectional acetate exchange couples ethanol turnover to acetyl-CoA metabolism in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
candidates.abstract: Overflow metabolism describes the excretion of partially oxidized metabolites into the extracellular environment during rapid sugar utilization. Although these metabolites can later be reused, it remains unclear whether reassimilation also occurs during ongoing sugar consumption, and if so, how. Here, 13C-isotope tracing and metabolic flux analysis of acetate exchange in Saccharomyces cerevisiae during hexose utilization reveal that net acetate overflow is only the small difference between order-of-magnitude larger simultaneous excretion and assimilation fluxes. Unlike ethanol production, acetate exchange is not determined by hexose uptake but depends on metabolic processes downstream of glycolysis. Ethanol oxidation contributes to acetate excretion even during net ethanol production, directly linking the two main overflow pathways. We exploited this understanding to redirect extracellular acetate into the acetyl-CoA-derived product mevalonate. These results establish acetate overflow as a dynamic exchange linking ethanol turnover to acetyl-CoA metabolism, in which acetate is simultaneously an overflow product and a carbon source that can be redirected toward bioproduction.

candidates.title: N- and T-genes framework for pathway deregulation: Taxonomy, progression, and protection in cancer
candidates.abstract: Background. Pathway analysis is widely used to interpret gene expression, but conventional enrichment depends on arbitrary thresholds and does not quantify deregulation magnitude. Recent reformulations based on average log-fold changes remove the threshold but still average over all annotated genes, diluting the signal from the genes that actually drive the normal-to-tumor transition. The N/T framework, which identifies genes with exclusive expression intervals in normal (N) or tumor (T) samples, offers a selective alternative, but it had not been extended to pathway- level quantification, taxonomy, or cross-cancer comparison. Methods. We define effective activation frequencies for Reactome pathways based on N- and T-genes: for each sample and pathway, the effective N (T) frequency is the fraction of annotated N (T) genes active in a normal (tumor) sample. The analysis proceeds in three explicit steps: (i) cohort averages identify the pathways important in each tissue; (ii) averages over hierarchical-clustering groups, ordered by the number of active genes, reveal sequences of pathway activation and deactivation along progression; (iii) a minimum spanning tree (MST) built on pathway-frequency vectors -- independent of the number of active genes -- defines the molecular taxonomy, and branch averages identify subtype-specific programs. We apply the framework to the full set of Reactome pathways in prostate adenocarcinoma (PRAD), lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC), and glioblastoma (GBM), analyzing both tumor and normal compartments. Results. In PRAD tumors (n=499), hierarchical clustering identifies four ordered progression groups and the MST resolves six main molecular subtypes comprising 406 tumors (81.4%): B1 (42.1%; MET/NFE2L2/energy metabolism), B2 (13.8%; RAS/apoptosis/telomere), and four smaller subtypes defined by PTEN (B3), DNA repair and lipid metabolism (B4), inflammation and LXR-mediated lipid metabolism (B5), and neuronal development and base excision repair (B6). An eight-gene perfect T panel reproduces the MST subtypes at gene level. Analysis of normal prostatic tissue (n=52) reveals a hierarchy of protection: immune response, apoptosis, and senescence are lost or partially lost early, DNA repair at an intermediate stage, and cell cycle regulation and receptor tyrosine kinase signaling last; an eleven-gene N panel reproduces this hierarchy at gene level. The cross-cancer comparison shows that this architecture is a general property: DNA repair, cell cycle, and RTK protection are maintained in normal tissue across PRAD, LUAD, LIHC, and GBM, while the specific pathways lost in normals and gained in tumors are tissue-specific (MET/NFE2L2 in PRAD; NTRK/LXR/phagosome in LIHC; surfactant/FGFR/glycosylation in LUAD; TP53loss/lipid metabolism/glycosylation in GBM). Taxonomic heterogeneity decreases from PRAD (six subtypes) to LIHC (two) to LUAD and GBM (one dominant program), paralleling an increase in the number of activated T-genes. Conclusions. The framework eliminates dilution by non-nformative genes, quantifies pathway deregulation sample by sample, and unifies tumor taxonomy with a molecular indicator of progression. Its most distinctive contribution is the joint analysis of normal and tumor compartments across cancer types, which links loss of protection in normal tissue to gain of progression programs in tumors and reveals both shared and tissue-specific cancer mechanisms. The method is general and applicable across cancer types, although quantitative results depend on the underlying cohort.

candidates.title: Fecal microbiota transplantation for pediatric Clostridioides difficile infection: efficacy, challenges, and the path to next-generation microbiome therapies.
candidates.abstract: Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) is an increasing cause of morbidity in children, with recurrent disease posing substantial therapeutic challenges. Antibiotic therapy remains the cornerstone of initial management; however, up to 30% of children experience recurrence, and those with underlying comorbidities face recurrence rates as high as 65%. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) has demonstrated superior efficacy over antibiotics for recurrent CDI (rCDI) in adults and has emerged as the most effective available intervention for pediatric rCDI. In this review, we synthesize current evidence on FMT efficacy, microbiome changes, and safety in children with CDI. Data from large multicenter cohort studies demonstrate cure rates exceeding 80%, with comparable efficacy observed in high-risk subpopulations, including those with inflammatory bowel disease and immunocompromising conditions. Critical research gaps remain, including the absence of randomized controlled trials and limited long-term safety data in children. Despite demonstrated effectiveness, significant barriers limit FMT accessibility for children. The COVID-19 pandemic has substantially impacted availability, and current regulatory changes have further restricted access. The lack of FDA-approved live biotherapeutic products approved for CDI in children creates additional challenges. We critically examine the emerging pipeline of next-generation microbiome-based therapies and identify the steps required to ensure children with recurrent CDI have access to safe, effective, and approved treatments.
candidates.article_body_excerpt:
[Background]
Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) is one of the leading healthcare-associated infections, with incidence rising over recent decades in both adults and children and an increasing shift toward community acquisition. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) has transformed the management of recurrent CDI (rCDI) in adults and demonstrated superiority over standard antibiotic therapy in randomized controlled trials (RCTs). 1 , 2 These compelling outcomes have prompted exploration of FMT in children with rCDI, where up to 30% of patients fail standard antibiotic therapy, and those with underlying conditions face recurrence rates as high as 65%. 3 Large observational studies have demonstrated FMT cure rates exceeding 80% in pediatric rCDI. However, recent restrictions on FMT access and the absence of approved microbiome-based live biotherapeutic products (LBPs) for patients under 18 have created a significant unmet need in children with recurrent and refractory disease. In this review, we discuss the rationale and efficacy of FMT for CDI in children, and critically examine the challenges – regulatory, biological, and therapeutic – that must be overcome to translate these findings into accessible, approved treatments for pediatric patients (Graphical abstract). This narrative review was conducted through a systematic search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library from inception through April 2026. The search terms included combinations of: “Clostridioides difficile,” “Clostridium difficile,” “CDI,” “fecal microbiota transplantation,” “FMT,” “live biotherapeutic product,” “pediatric,” “children,” and “recurrent.” Reference lists of identified articles were reviewed for additional relevant studies. The inclusion criteria encompassed clinical trials, cohort studies, case series, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and guidelines pertaining to pediatric CDI or FMT in children. Studies exclusively in adults were included where pediatric data were absent or to provide contextual comparison.

[Clostridioides difficile infection in children]
Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) is a gram-positive anaerobic bacterium that produces highly resistant spores that are transmitted via the fecal-oral route and can persist in healthcare and community environments, leading to widespread infections. 4 , 5 CDI produces a wide clinical spectrum ranging from mild diarrhea to severe hemorrhagic colitis, with potentially life-threatening complications, including toxic megacolon and death. 4 , 6 Antibiotic use, increasing age, and underlying comorbidities that promote gut dysbiosis all heighten susceptibility.
CDI rates rose dramatically from the 1990s in both adults and children, emerging as a global public health threat. 7 CDI was initially considered a predominantly healthcare associated (HA) illness, however a large U.S. study demonstrated a significant decrease from 7.09 HA-CDI pediatric cases per 10,000 patient days in 2013 to 4.89 cases per 10,000 patient-days in 2019 while community acquired (CA) CDI rates increased from 9.6/100,000 children per year in 2012 to peak at 16.9/100,000 children per year in 2015. 8 , 9 Subsequently, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Emerging Infections Program confirmed that the incidence of CA-CDI surpassed HA-CDI across all age groups, including children ages 1–17 y old where the incidence of CA-CDI is 21/100,000 persons and HA-CDI is 8.1/100,000 persons. 10 This shift likely reflects the adoption of robust infection control and antimicrobial stewardship measures in healthcare settings. 11 , 12
The most common risk factor for CDI in children is antibiotic exposure, particularly with clindamycin, third-generation cephalosporins, and fluoroquinolones. 13 , 14 Although most children with CDI report antibiotic exposure in the preceding 4 weeks, many have no prior antibiotic exposure, especially among those with CA-CDI. 15 Additionally, multiple courses of antibiotics further increase the risk of CDI (OR 1.93, 95% CI 1.25–2.97). 16 Acid suppressants, specifically proton pump inhibitors, also increase CDI risk, likely through their effects on the gut microbiome. 14 , 16 , 17 Prior hospitalization, length of hospitalization, and even recent outpatient visits are additional risk factors, underscoring the ongoing importance of infection control in pediatric settings. 14 Approximately 30%–50% of children who develop CDI have significant underlying comorbidities, including prior solid organ transplantation, immunodeficiency, malignancy, and inflammatory bowel d

[Current non-FMT treatment options]
The first step in management, regardless of the therapeutic agent being used, is discontinuation of the inciting antibiotic when able. Pediatric treatment guidelines from 2017 recommend that first-line antibiotic therapy for non-severe initial CDI or first recurrence in children includes oral metronidazole (7.5 mg/kg/dose three or four times daily for 10 d) or oral vancomycin (10 mg/kg/dose four times daily for 10 d). 34 A systematic review and meta-analysis of pediatric observational studies demonstrated significantly lower cure rates with metronidazole compared to vancomycin, consistent with adult data, and has driven increasing use of vancomycin in pediatric practice. 8 , 43 Metronidazole has been progressively de-prioritized in both adult and pediatric practice owing to inferior efficacy, increasing clinical failure rates, and palatability challenges from its metallic taste; its use is now generally discouraged except where access to alternatives is limited. For severe initial CDI, oral or rectal vancomycin, with or without intravenous metronidazole (10 mg/kg/dose three times daily), is recommended. For second or subsequent recurrences, recommended regimens include a tapered and pulsed vancomycin course over at least 6 weeks or vancomycin for 10 d followed by rifaximin for 20 d, with FMT as an alternative. 34 A shared limitation of these regimens is their frequent dosing, which has been consistently associated with reduced medication adherence. 44
While the 2021 adult CDI guidelines recommend fidaxomicin as first-line therapy for initial or rCDI, the pediatric IDSA/SHEA guidelines, last updated in 2017, do not yet reflect this recommendation. 34 , 45 However, compelling pediatric data exist. The SUNSHINE trial, a phase 3, multicenter RCT, compared fidaxomicin (oral suspension 16 mg/kg/dose twice daily for children under 6 y, or 200 mg tablets twice daily for older children) to vancomycin for 10 d in patients under 18 y of age. 46 Fidaxomicin demonstrated significantly higher rates of global cure, i.e., confirmed clinical response without rCDI until the time of assessment. A real-world, retrospective pediatric multicenter study supports these findings, showing that fidaxomicin is well-tolerated with a 78.5% cure rate without relapse at day 60. 47 Fidaxomicin’s twice-daily dosing and lower rCDI rate also make it an appealing option. [Rationale for FMT in pediatric CDI]
Gut dysbiosis plays a central role in CDI pathogenesis. Disruption of the commensal gut microbiota, most commonly by antibiotic exposure, permits CD colonization, proliferation, and toxin production. Despite a small number of effective treatments, rCDI is a common challenge in children, necessitating the need for FMT. 37-40
FMT is defined as the transfer of fecal material from a healthy screened donor into a patient with rCDI, with the goal of restoring microbial diversity and re-establishing colonization resistance against CD. 57 While the exact mechanism of clearance of C. difficile through FMT remains unclear, observed microbiome changes include: (1) relative increase in abundance of Bacteroidetes and decreased abundance of Proteobacteria; (2) increased diversity of the microbial communities; (3) post-FMT similarities between the patients’ microbiome and the donor flora; and (4) restoration of normal fecal bile acid composition. 58-60 FMT is now considered the standard of care for patients with rCDI non-responsive to antibiotics. 61
FMT was first described in the English literature in 1958 in adults with pseudomembranous enterocolitis. 62 The landmark RCT by van Nood et al. in 2013 demonstrated FMT superiority over vancomycin for rCDI (81% vs. 31% cure rate), 59 and numerous subsequent RCTs, observational studies, and registry data have confirmed FMT efficacy in adults with cure rates exceeding 90%. 1 , 63-67 The first reported pediatric FMT via nasogastric tube was in 2010, and the first colonoscopic FMT in a child was in 2012. 68 , 69
FMT for Recurrent CDI: The primary and best-evidenced indication for FMT in children is prevention of further episodes in those with rCDI – defined as two or more recurrences after an initial treated episode. The rationale is the restoration of gut microbial diversity and colonization resistance, disrupted by repeated antibiotic courses as per adults. Large pediatric cohorts confirm cure rates exceeding 80% for this indication, as discussed in detail below. 3 RCTs are not available in children.
FMT for severe, fulminant, or refractory CDI: FMT has also been used as rescue therapy in children with severe or fulminant CDI unresponsive to antibiotics, or in those with refractory disease. Evidence for this indication in children is limited to case reports and small series. 70 The physiologic rationale –rapid microbiome reconstitution to interrupt toxin-mediated colonic injury and potentially the immune-modulating effect of F

[Effectiveness and safety of FMT in pediatric CDI]
To date, no prospective RCTs have evaluated the use of FMT in children with CDI, representing a significant gap in the evidence base. Current evidence is limited to retrospective studies and single-center cohort studies (Table 1).

candidates.title: A specialized microbiome enriched in nitrification and halogen cycling potential resolved from multi-omics investigation of a Caribbean suboxic and acidic marine sinkhole.
candidates.abstract: Background The Luymes Sinkholes, located on the Luymes Bank northwest of Saba, represent a unique marine environment characterized by distinct biogeochemical gradients. Most noticeable is an acidic (pH ≈ 6.25) and suboxic (O2 Results We identified a distinct microbial community within the submerged acid lake different from the non-acidic sinkholes, with increased abundances of Nitrospinota, Thermoproteota, Planctomycetota, and Actinobacteriota. We also found three enriched classes of dissolved compounds within the submerged acid lake: (1) large, (2) low-polarity, and (3) halogenated metabolites, including iodides and halobenzoic acids. Correlations between microbial taxa and metabolite classes show potential links between nitrifying archaea and halogenated compound cycling. We further supported these findings using the functional annotation of metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) and protein clusters showing enrichment of nitrification and halogen cycling genes, suggesting the presence of specialized degradation and biosynthetic pathways, directly connecting microbial metabolism to the observed geochemical conditions. Conclusion These findings demonstrate that the submerged acid lake contains specific microbially driven biogeochemical processes under acidified and low-oxygen conditions, providing a natural model for future extreme ocean acidification scenarios. With this multi‑omics approach, we were able to connect the microbial metabolism with this unique environment, thereby expanding our understanding of how both are interconnected. Video Abstract.
